```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(tidymodels)
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)
source(here::here("R/theme.R"))
source(here::here("R/data.R"))
set.seed(2026)

# A number for the prose, with a true minus sign.
num <- function(x, digits) sub("^-", "−", format(round(x, digits), nsmall = digits))
```

## Maximum likelihood trusts every station

[Maximum likelihood](maximum-likelihood.qmd) chooses the parameters that make the data
most probable, and it looks at nothing but the data. With many stations that is a
strength. With a small survey and many inputs, it reports whatever those few stations
happen to show, including effects far larger than any the species could have.

You usually know better. From earlier surveys and the literature, you know roughly how
large an effect can be. This page shows how to add that knowledge to the fit, and that
the result is **ridge regression**, a method that
[section 5](../05-generalisation/regularisation.qmd) uses to stop models overfitting.

{{< include ../../_snippets/simulated-data.qmd >}}

## A prior says how large effects usually are

A **prior** is what you believe about a parameter before seeing the data, written as a
distribution. "The effect of one standard deviation of temperature is usually within
about ±2 animals, and very rarely ±9" is a prior on the temperature coefficient. It is
a statement about scale, not a claim to know the answer.

**Maximum a posteriori** (MAP) estimation adds the prior to the likelihood. It chooses
the parameters that make the data probable *and* are plausible under the prior. The
result is a compromise between the two, and the one that is more certain wins more of
it. Many stations outweigh a loose prior; a few stations get pulled towards it. The
distribution that combines them is the **posterior**, and the MAP estimate is its
highest point.

## A Normal prior is the ridge penalty

[Maximum likelihood](maximum-likelihood.qmd) turned the likelihood into a loss by taking
its negative log. Do the same with a prior, and it becomes a **penalty**: a second term
added to the loss that grows as the coefficients move away from zero.

A Normal prior centred on zero gives a penalty equal to the sum of the squared
coefficients, times a weight called λ (lambda). Least squares plus that penalty is ridge
regression. λ is the noise variance divided by the prior's variance: noisy data or a
tight prior make λ large and pull the coefficients harder towards zero.

Other priors give other penalties. A Laplace prior, with a sharp peak at zero, gives the
**lasso**, which section 5 uses to drop inputs altogether. A flat prior, which treats
every value as equally plausible, gives no penalty at all, and that is maximum
likelihood. Maximum likelihood is not free of assumptions: it assumes a coefficient of
900 is as plausible as one of 0.9.

::: {.diagram}
![A flat prior gives no penalty, which is maximum likelihood. A Normal prior centred on zero gives the squared penalty of ridge regression, which shrinks every coefficient but sets none to zero. A Laplace prior gives the absolute penalty of the lasso, which can set some coefficients to zero.](img/priors-to-penalties.svg){fig-alt="Three cards. Flat prior, gives no penalty, maximum likelihood: a level line across the coefficient axis; a coefficient of 900 is as plausible as one of 0.9. Normal prior, gives the squared penalty, ridge regression: a bell curve centred on zero; most effects small, shrinks every coefficient but zeroes none. Laplace prior, gives the absolute penalty, lasso: a sharp peak at zero; can set some coefficients to zero. A note says: choose a prior on the coefficients, and its negative log is the penalty."}
:::

The prior says how large a coefficient is per unit of its input, so the inputs must be on
a common scale first. A prior of ±2 animals per metre of depth and ±2 per millimetre
would be two very different beliefs. Ridge regression standardises every input to a
standard deviation of 1 before fitting, for the same reason
[Gradient descent](gradient-descent.qmd) did.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The maths, if you want it

MAP maximises the log-likelihood plus the log-prior:

$$\hat\beta_{\text{MAP}} = \arg\max_\beta \; \log p(y \mid \beta) + \log p(\beta)$$

With a Normal response of standard deviation $\sigma$ and a Normal prior
$\beta_j \sim \text{Normal}(0, \tau)$ on each coefficient, this is

$$-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_i (y_i - x_i^\top\beta)^2 \;-\; \frac{1}{2\tau^2}\sum_j \beta_j^2 + \text{const}$$

Multiply by $-2\sigma^2$, and maximising it becomes minimising

$$\sum_i (y_i - x_i^\top\beta)^2 + \lambda \sum_j \beta_j^2, \qquad \lambda = \frac{\sigma^2}{\tau^2}$$

which is the ridge objective. A Laplace prior puts $\lvert\beta_j\rvert$ in place of
$\beta_j^2$, which is the lasso.
:::

## Worked example

### Forty stations and twelve inputs

A pilot survey might have forty stations. We draw forty at random and fit abundance on
twelve inputs: depth and temperature with their squares, chlorophyll, salinity, and
substrate and season as dummy columns. The other stations are held back as a test set.
Every input is standardised on the forty training stations, so each coefficient is the
change in abundance for one standard deviation of its input.

```{r}
#| label: prepare
survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean()

d <- survey |>
  select(abundance, depth_m, temperature_c, chlorophyll_mg_m3,
         salinity_psu, substrate, season) |>
  drop_na()

X_all <- model.matrix(
  ~ depth_m + I(depth_m^2) + temperature_c + I(temperature_c^2) +
    chlorophyll_mg_m3 + salinity_psu + substrate + season,
  data = d
)[, -1]

train_rows <- sample(nrow(d), 40)

# Standardise with the training stations only, and centre abundance on
# their mean, so the model needs no intercept.
centre <- colMeans(X_all[train_rows, ])
spread <- apply(X_all[train_rows, ], 2, sd)
X <- scale(X_all, centre, spread)
y <- d$abundance - mean(d$abundance[train_rows])

X_train <- X[train_rows, ];  y_train <- y[train_rows]
X_test  <- X[-train_rows, ]; y_test  <- y[-train_rows]

mle_fit <- lm(y_train ~ X_train - 1)
mle <- summary(mle_fit)$coefficients
rownames(mle) <- colnames(X)
round(mle[, 1:2], 2)
```

```{r}
#| label: mle-numbers
#| include: false
b_temp  <- mle["temperature_c", 1]
se_temp <- mle["temperature_c", 2]
b_temp2 <- mle["I(temperature_c^2)", 1]
```

Temperature gets `r num(b_temp, 2)` animals per standard deviation and its square
`r num(b_temp2, 2)`. Those are two closely related columns taking large opposite values
that partly cancel, and the standard error of the temperature coefficient is
`r num(se_temp, 2)`: the forty stations barely tell `r num(b_temp, 2)` apart from zero.
Maximum likelihood reports it anyway.

### A tighter prior pulls harder

```{r}
#| label: fig-prior-likelihood
#| fig-cap: !expr glue::glue("Prior, likelihood and posterior for the temperature coefficient on its own. The likelihood (grey) peaks at {num(b_temp, 2)} but is very wide. As the prior tightens from left to right, the posterior peak moves towards zero, to {num(peaks[1], 2)}, then {num(peaks[2], 2)}, then {num(peaks[3], 2)}.")
#| fig-alt: !expr glue::glue("Three side-by-side panels, each with three curves against the temperature coefficient. In every panel a broad, flat grey likelihood curve peaks at {num(b_temp, 2)}. An orange prior curve centred on zero narrows from panel to panel, and a blue posterior curve sits between the two. The posterior peak is at {num(peaks[1], 2)} in the left panel, {num(peaks[2], 2)} in the middle and {num(peaks[3], 2)} on the right, where it almost matches the prior.")
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.4
prior_sds <- c(5, 1, 0.5)
peaks <- b_temp * prior_sds^2 / (prior_sds^2 + se_temp^2)
panel_names <- sprintf("prior sd %.1f, peak at %.2f", prior_sds, peaks)

curves <- map2_dfr(prior_sds, panel_names, \(tau, panel) {
  b <- seq(-5, 15, length.out = 500)
  peak <- b_temp * tau^2 / (tau^2 + se_temp^2)
  tibble(
    b,
    Likelihood = dnorm(b, b_temp, se_temp),
    Prior      = dnorm(b, 0, tau),
    Posterior  = dnorm(b, peak, sqrt(1 / (1 / se_temp^2 + 1 / tau^2))),
    panel = factor(panel, levels = panel_names)
  )
}) |>
  pivot_longer(c(Likelihood, Prior, Posterior), names_to = "curve",
               values_to = "density")

ggplot(curves, aes(b, density, colour = curve)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(
    Likelihood = ml_palette[["grey"]],
    Prior      = ml_palette[["orange"]],
    Posterior  = ml_palette[["blue"]]
  )) +
  labs(x = "Temperature coefficient", y = NULL, colour = NULL,
       title = "The posterior sits between the prior and the likelihood") +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank())
```

A prior with a standard deviation of 5 barely objects to `r num(b_temp, 2)` and moves
the estimate to `r num(peaks[1], 2)`. A prior of 1, the belief that effects are usually
within about ±2, moves it to `r num(peaks[2], 2)`. The data never supported a large
effect, and even a loose prior is enough to say so. The figure treats temperature alone;
the full fit below shrinks all twelve coefficients together, so its numbers differ a
little.

### MAP and ridge give the same coefficients

We fit MAP directly with `optim()`, using a Normal likelihood and a Normal prior with a
standard deviation of 1 on every coefficient. For the noise standard deviation we use
the residual standard deviation of the maximum-likelihood fit. Then we fit ridge
regression by its formula, with λ equal to the noise variance over the prior variance.

```{r}
#| label: map-equals-ridge
sigma <- summary(mle_fit)$sigma   # noise sd, from the unpenalised fit
tau   <- 1                        # prior sd on each coefficient

neg_log_posterior <- function(b) {
  -sum(dnorm(y_train, X_train %*% b, sigma, log = TRUE)) -
    sum(dnorm(b, 0, tau, log = TRUE))
}

map_fit <- optim(rep(0, ncol(X_train)), neg_log_posterior, method = "BFGS",
                 control = list(reltol = 1e-14, maxit = 10000))

ridge <- function(lambda) {
  drop(solve(t(X_train) %*% X_train + lambda * diag(ncol(X_train)),
             t(X_train) %*% y_train))
}

lambda <- sigma^2 / tau^2
coefs <- tibble(
  term  = colnames(X_train),
  MLE   = ridge(0),
  MAP   = map_fit$par,
  ridge = ridge(lambda)
)
coefs |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

```{r}
#| label: map-numbers
#| include: false
map_ridge_gap <- max(abs(coefs$MAP - coefs$ridge))
agree_places <- floor(-log10(map_ridge_gap))
temp_map  <- coefs$ridge[coefs$term == "temperature_c"]
temp2_map <- coefs$ridge[coefs$term == "I(temperature_c^2)"]
```

The MAP and ridge columns agree to `r agree_places` decimal places: the same answer
reached from two directions, with λ = `r num(lambda, 1)`. Setting λ to zero
gives back maximum likelihood, the first column. The temperature pair falls from
`r num(b_temp, 2)` and `r num(b_temp2, 2)` to `r num(temp_map, 2)` and
`r num(temp2_map, 2)`.

### A prior improves prediction

A prior makes the fit to the forty stations worse, since it pulls the coefficients away
from the values that fit them best. The test is whether it predicts the other stations
better. We fit ridge regression over a range of λ and measure the RMSE on both sets.

```{r}
#| label: lambda-curve
rmse <- function(b, X, y) sqrt(mean((y - X %*% b)^2))

curve <- tibble(lambda = exp(seq(log(0.01), log(500), length.out = 120))) |>
  mutate(
    b     = map(lambda, ridge),
    train = map_dbl(b, rmse, X = X_train, y = y_train),
    test  = map_dbl(b, rmse, X = X_test,  y = y_test)
  )

mean_only <- sqrt(mean(y_test^2))   # predict the training mean everywhere
best <- curve |> slice_min(test)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-lambda
#| fig-cap: !expr glue::glue("Training and test RMSE against λ for the forty-station fit. Training error rises as λ grows. Test error falls to its lowest near λ = {round(best$lambda)} and then rises again. The dashed line is the error from predicting the training mean at every station.")
#| fig-alt: !expr glue::glue("Two curves against lambda from 0.01 to 500 on a logarithmic horizontal axis. The training curve starts at {num(curve$train[1], 2)} and rises steadily. The test curve starts at {num(curve$test[1], 2)}, dips to {num(best$test, 2)} near lambda {round(best$lambda)}, then rises again. A dashed horizontal line at {num(mean_only, 2)} marks the error of predicting the mean.")
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.3
curve |>
  select(lambda, Training = train, Test = test) |>
  pivot_longer(-lambda, names_to = "set", values_to = "rmse") |>
  ggplot(aes(lambda, rmse, colour = set)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean_only, linetype = "dashed",
             colour = ml_palette[["grey"]]) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_number()) +
  labs(
    x = "λ (log scale)", y = "RMSE (animals)", colour = NULL,
    title = "The prior costs training fit and buys test accuracy",
    subtitle = "Dashed line: predicting the training mean everywhere"
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: gains
#| include: false
map_test <- rmse(ridge(lambda), X_test, y_test)
gain <- function(e) 1 - e / mean_only
```

Predicting the training mean at every station gives a test RMSE of
`r num(mean_only, 2)`. Maximum likelihood with twelve inputs gives
`r num(curve$test[1], 2)`, only `r scales::percent(gain(curve$test[1]), 0.1)` better.
The prior with a standard deviation of 1 gives `r num(map_test, 2)`,
`r scales::percent(gain(map_test), 0.1)` better, from the same stations and inputs.

The two curves carry the main idea of section 5:

- **Training error only rises with λ.** Every step pulls the fit further from the
  forty stations.
- **Test error falls, then rises.** A small λ removes more noise than pattern; a large
  one flattens the real effects too.
- **The training curve cannot choose λ.** It has no low point. λ is a hyperparameter,
  and [Hyperparameter selection](../05-generalisation/hyperparameter-selection.qmd)
  chooses it on held-out data.

Here the test set drew the curve, which is fine for showing its shape but would be
cheating as a way of choosing λ.

## Ridge shrinks but never removes

```{r}
#| label: smallest
#| include: false
smallest <- coefs |> slice_min(abs(ridge))
labels <- c(
  depth_m = "depth", `I(depth_m^2)` = "depth squared",
  temperature_c = "temperature", `I(temperature_c^2)` = "temperature squared",
  chlorophyll_mg_m3 = "chlorophyll", salinity_psu = "salinity",
  substratemud = "mud substrate", substraterock = "rock substrate",
  substratesand = "sand substrate", seasonsummer = "summer",
  seasonautumn = "autumn", seasonwinter = "winter"
)
```

No coefficient in the ridge fit is exactly zero. The smallest, for
`r labels[[smallest$term]]`, is `r num(smallest$ridge, 3)`. A
Normal prior pulls every coefficient towards zero but never onto it, so ridge regression
cannot tell you an input is irrelevant. The lasso's Laplace prior can, and
[Regularisation](../05-generalisation/regularisation.qmd) in section 5 uses it that way.

MAP also gives a single best value, not a range. A full Bayesian analysis keeps the
whole posterior, which gives honest intervals; a ridge fit gives the shrinkage without
the intervals. And once λ is chosen from the data, as section 5 does, it is no longer a
belief held before the survey, so report it as a tuned setting.

## Key points

::: {.key-points}
- A **prior** states how large a parameter is likely to be before the data arrive;
  **MAP** chooses the parameters that fit the data and are plausible under the prior.
- A Normal prior on the coefficients is the ridge penalty, with λ equal to the noise
  variance over the prior variance. Here MAP and ridge agreed to
  `r agree_places` decimal places.
- A Laplace prior gives the lasso, and a flat prior gives maximum likelihood.
- Priors are stated per standard deviation of each input, so standardise first.
- On forty stations, maximum likelihood beat predicting the mean by
  `r scales::percent(gain(curve$test[1]), 0.1)` and MAP by
  `r scales::percent(gain(map_test), 0.1)`.
- Training error only rises with λ, so λ has to be chosen on held-out data.
:::

## Try it yourself

1. Double `sigma` and refit, leaving `tau` alone. Predict first which way the
   coefficients move, then check against λ = σ²/τ².
2. Replace the Normal prior in `neg_log_posterior()` with a Laplace one,
   `sum(abs(b)) / tau` in place of the `dnorm()` term, and refit. Do any coefficients
   reach exactly zero?
